claim: RSL class I bHLH transcription factors control a gene regulatory network that positively regulates the development of filamentous rooting cells (root hairs and rhizoids) in land plants.
source: Basic helix-loop-helix transcription factors encoded by RSL class I genes control a gene regulatory network that positively regulates the development of filamentous rooting cells – root hairs and rhizoids – in land plants.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work and experimental data presented in the manuscript regarding RSL class I gene function.

claim: GLABRA2 transcription factor negatively regulates RSL class I genes in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: The GLABRA2 transcription factor negatively regulates these genes in the angiosperm Arabidopsis thaliana.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on GLABRA2 function.

claim: FEW RHIZOIDS1 (MpFRH1) microRNA negatively regulates the RSL class I gene MpRSL1 in Marchantia polymorpha.
source: This identified FEW RHIZOIDS1 (MpFRH1) microRNA (miRNA) that negatively regulates the RSL class I gene Mp RSL1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from mutant screens, qRT-PCR, and functional assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: MpFRH1 miRNA and its mRNA target constitute a feedback mechanism that controls epidermal cell differentiation.
source: The miRNA and its mRNA target constitute a feedback mechanism that controls epidermal cell differentiation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing MpRSL1 positively regulates MpFRH1 expression (Figure 6).

claim: MpFRH1 miRNA target sites are conserved among liverwort RSL class I mRNAs but are not present in RSL class I mRNAs of other land plants.
source: MpFRH1 miRNA target sites are conserved among liverwort RSL class I mRNAs but are not present in RSL class I mRNAs of other land plants.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data showing 100% conservation in twelve liverwort species (Figure 8) and absence in other lineages.

claim: Independent negative regulatory mechanisms evolved in different lineages during land plant evolution to regulate RSL class I genes.
source: These findings indicate that while RSL class I genes are ancient and conserved, independent negative regulatory mechanisms evolved in different lineages during land plant evolution.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that liverworts use miRNA while Arabidopsis uses GL2 protein for negative regulation.

claim: The first land plants colonized the land sometime more than 470 million years ago.
source: The evolution of specialised rooting structures were key morphological innovations that occurred among the first plants when they colonised the land sometime more than 470 Million years ago (Kenrick and Crane, 1997; Morris et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to paleontological literature.

claim: The rooting structures of the first land plants likely comprised systems of tip-growing filamentous cells called rhizoids that are morphologically similar to root hairs of vascular plants.
source: The rooting structures of the first land plants are likely to have comprised systems of tip-growing filamentous cells called rhizoids that are morphologically similar to root hairs of vascular plants (Edwards et al., 1995; Wellman et al., 2003; Taylor et al., 2005; Kerp et al., 2003; Taylor, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to paleobotanical studies.

claim: RSL class I genes promote root hair differentiation in rice (Oryza sativa), Brachypodium distachyon, and Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: RSL class I genes promote root hair differentiation in the vascular plants rice (Oryza sativa), Brachypodium distachyon and Arabidopsis thaliana (Zalewski et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017; Menand et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: RSL class I genes positively regulate rhizoid precursor cell differentiation and rhizoid development in Marchantia polymorpha and Physcomitrella patens.
source: Similarly, RSL class I genes positively regulate rhizoid precursor cell differentiation and rhizoid development in the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha and the moss Physcomitrella patens (Proust et al., 2016; Menand et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Root hairs and rhizoids initiate from epidermal cells that express RSL class I genes.
source: Root hairs and rhizoids initiate from those epidermal cells that express RSL class I genes (Zalewski et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017; Menand et al., 2007; Jang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Constitutive over-expression of RSL class I genes is sufficient to induce root hair development from any root epidermal cell in monocots O. sativa and B. distachyon.
source: Furthermore, constitutive over-expression of RSL class I genes is sufficient to modulate root hair patterning by inducing root hair development from any root epidermal cell in the monocots O. sativa and B. distachyon (Zalewski et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Constitutive over-expression of RSL class I genes in M. polymorpha and P. patens is sufficient to induce rhizoid formation from almost any epidermal cell of the gametophyte.
source: Similarly, constitutive over-expression of RSL class I genes in the liverwort M. polymorpha and moss P. patens is sufficient to induce rhizoid formation from almost any epidermal cell of the gametophyte (Proust et al., 2016; Jang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: RSL class I genes function as molecular switches that are both necessary and sufficient to induce the root hair cell and rhizoid cell developmental program in epidermal cells.
source: These findings indicate that RSL class I genes function as molecular switches that are both necessary and sufficient to induce the root hair cell and rhizoid cell developmental program in epidermal cells.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental evidence cited showing necessity and sufficiency of RSL class I genes.

claim: The function of RSL class I genes in regulating the development of filamentous rooting cells is conserved among land plants.
source: The demonstration that the RSL class I genes are required for rhizoid and root hair development indicates that their function in regulating the development of filamentous rooting cells is conserved among land plants.
evidence: Inferred from conservation of function across multiple lineages as documented by citations.

claim: The RSL class I mechanism is likely ancient and originated in the common ancestor of all land plants.
source: This suggests that the RSL class I mechanism is likely to be ancient and have originated in the common ancestor of all land plants.
evidence: Speculative inference based on conservation across land plant lineages.

claim: RSL class I genes from P. patens, M. polymorpha, or rice restore root hair development in roothairless A. thaliana mutants that lack RSL class I gene function.
source: RSL class I genes from the moss P. patens, liverwort M. polymorpha or monocot rice restore root hair development in the roothairless A. thaliana mutants that lack RSL class I gene function (Menand et al., 2007; Proust et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies demonstrating functional complementation.

claim: The molecular function of RSL class I proteins is conserved among moss, liverwort, monocot, and dicot lineages.
source: This indicates that the molecular function of RSL class I proteins is conserved among these lineages.
evidence: Inferred from functional complementation experiments cited.

claim: Negative regulation of RSL class I genes in A. thaliana suppresses the formation of root hairs in a subset of root epidermal cells.
source: Negative regulation of RSL class I genes in A. thaliana suppresses the formation of root hairs in a subset of root epidermal cells (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior experimental study.

claim: The A. thaliana root epidermis comprises two cell types: trichoblasts that differentiate into root hair cells and atrichoblasts that differentiate as root hairless epidermal cells.
source: The A. thaliana root epidermis comprises two cell types; trichoblasts that go on to differentiate into root hair cells and atrichoblasts that differentiate as root hairless epidermal cells.
evidence: Established knowledge about Arabidopsis root epidermis cell types.

claim: AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 are expressed early in development of trichoblasts before root hairs emerge and positively regulate genes involved in root hair differentiation.
source: RSL class I genes, AtRHD6 and AtRSL1, are expressed early in development of trichoblasts before root hairs emerge and they positively regulate the expression of genes involved in root hair differentiation (Menand et al., 2007; Yi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 expression is repressed in atrichoblasts by the homeodomain protein GLABRA2 (GL2).
source: AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 expression is repressed in atrichoblasts by the homeodomain protein GLABRA2 (GL2) (Di Cristina et al., 1996; Bernhardt et al., 2005; Bernhardt et al., 2003; Koshino-Kimura et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: AtGL2 proteins directly bind to L1 box motifs on the promoters of AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 and inhibit root hair initiation by repressing transcription of these genes.
source: AtGL2 proteins directly bind to L1 box motifs on the promoters of AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 and inhibit root hair initiation by repressing the transcription of these positive regulators of root hair development (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior experimental study.

claim: The role of GL2 as negative regulator of RSL class I genes and root hair development is not likely to be widely conserved because the closest homologs of GL2 in many other vascular plants are not expressed in roots.
source: However, the role of GL2 as negative regulator of RSL class I genes and root hair development is not likely to be widely conserved because the closest homologs of GL2 in many other vascular plants are not expressed in roots (Huang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study on GL2 homolog expression patterns.

claim: GL2 genes have not been identified in bryophytes (liverworts, mosses and hornworts).
source: Furthermore, GL2 genes have not been identified in bryophytes (liverworts, mosses and hornworts) (Zalewski et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Four mutants (ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2, and ST49-10) develop no or very few rhizoid precursor cells and consequently develop few rhizoids.
source: We identified four mutants, ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2 and ST49-10 that develop no or very few rhizoid precursor cells and consequently develop few rhizoids (Figure 1A–L).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and microscopy images in Figure 1.

claim: The few rhizoids phenotype segregated as a single locus in F1 generations of ST45-2 and ST49-10 backcrosses.
source: The few rhizoids phenotype segregated as a single locus in each F1 generation, that is 50% of plants developed few rhizoids and 50% were indistinguishable from wild type (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by genetic segregation data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The few rhizoids phenotype co-segregated with the hygromycin resistance marker gene on the T-DNA in both ST45-2 and ST49-10 segregating F1 populations.
source: Furthermore, the few rhizoids phenotype co-segregated with the hygromycin resistance marker gene on the T-DNA in both ST45-2 and ST49-10 segregating F1 populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by genetic co-segregation data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a single T-DNA insertion tightly linked to the few rhizoids phenotype in ST45-2.
source: Based on the ratios of hygromycin resistant to hygromycin sensitive F1 plants, there is a single T-DNA insertion that is tightly linked to the few rhizoids phenotype in ST45-2.
evidence: Inferred from genetic segregation ratios.

claim: ST49-10 has two T-DNA insertions; one responsible for the few rhizoids phenotype and a second unlinked T-DNA insertion.
source: There are two T-DNA insertions in ST49-10; one responsible for the few rhizoids phenotype and a second unlinked T-DNA insertion.
evidence: Inferred from genetic segregation ratios.

claim: A T-DNA insertion was identified within a 1.2 kb region of the M. polymorpha genome in each of the four few rhizoids mutants ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2, and ST49-10.
source: We identified a T-DNA insertion within a 1.2 kb region of the M. polymorpha genome in each of the few rhizoids mutants ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2 and ST49-10 (Figure 1M, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Supported by TAIL-PCR data presented in Figure 1M and Supplementary file 1.

claim: No transcript overlapped with the T-DNA insertion sites in any of the four few rhizoids mutants based on transcriptome mapping.
source: Mapping the M. polymorpha gametophyte transcriptome sequences onto the genome assembly (Honkanen et al., 2016) indicated that no transcript overlapped with the T-DNA insertion sites in any of the four few rhizoids mutants.
evidence: Supported by bioinformatic analysis of transcriptome data.

claim: A transcript fragment that mapped next to the right border of the T-DNA insertions was expressed at higher levels in each of the few rhizoids mutants ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2, and ST49-10 than in wild type.
source: A transcript fragment that mapped next to the right border of the T-DNA insertions was expressed at higher levels in each of the few rhizoids mutants ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2 and ST49-10 than in wild type (Figure 1N).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 1N.

claim: 3' and 5' RACE-PCR identified a 1.2 kb intron-less polyadenylated transcript named FEW RHIZOIDS1 (MpFRH1).
source: To identify the full-length transcript we performed 3' and 5' RACE-PCR. This identified a 1.2 kb intron-less polyadenylated transcript (Supplementary file 2) that we named FEW RHIZOIDS1 (MpFRH1).
evidence: Supported by RACE-PCR experimental data.

claim: In each of the four few rhizoids mutants, a T-DNA is inserted 5' of a gene encoding a 1.2 kb transcript that is expressed at higher levels than in wild type.
source: Together these data indicate that in each of the four few rhizoids mutants a T-DNA is inserted 5' of a gene encoding a 1.2 kb transcript that is expressed at higher levels than in wild type.
evidence: Inferred from T-DNA insertion mapping and expression data.

claim: The majority of transformed plants (88 out of 103) expressing MpFRH1 under the rice ACTIN1 promoter developed very few or no rhizoids.
source: The majority of the resulting transformed plants (88 out of 103) developed very few or no rhizoids (Figure 2C,G,K).
evidence: Supported by transformation experiments and phenotypic observations in Figure 2.

claim: Steady state levels of MpFRH1 transcript were higher than wild type in each of the transformed lines with few rhizoids.
source: Steady state levels of MpFRH1 transcript were higher than wild type in each of the transformed lines with few rhizoids, while wild type levels of MpFRH1 transcript were observed in the lines with wild type phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Over-expression of the 1.2 kb MpFRH1 transcript in the wild type background was sufficient to reproduce the few rhizoids phenotype of the T-DNA insertion mutants.
source: This indicates that over-expression of the 1.2 kb MpFRH1 transcript in the wild type background was sufficient to reproduce the few rhizoids phenotype of the ST21-1, ST49-10, ST45-2 and ST33-2 T-DNA insertion mutants.
evidence: Inferred from transformation experiments showing phenocopy.

claim: ST21-1, ST49-10, ST45-2, and ST33-2 are gain-of-function mutants in which elevated expression of MpFRH1 results in reduced number of rhizoid precursor cells and rhizoids.
source: This suggests that each is a gain-of-function mutant, in which elevated expression of MpFRH1 results in reduced number of rhizoid precursor cells and rhizoids.
evidence: Inferred from overexpression experiments and mutant phenotypes.

claim: MpFRH1 is a negative regulator of rhizoid precursor cell differentiation.
source: Together these findings indicate that MpFRH1 is a negative regulator of rhizoid precursor cell differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from gain-of-function mutant phenotypes and overexpression experiments.

claim: MpFRH1 gain-of-function mutants and proACT:MpFRH1 lines are defective in the formation of gemmae and epidermal papillae, similar to Mprsl1 loss-of-function mutants.
source: While MpFRH1 gain-of-function mutants and proACT:MpFRH1 lines develop few rhizoids like Mprsl1, they were also defective in the formation of other structures that originate from single epidermal cells... gemmae only rarely develop in Mprsl1, MpFRH1GOF, proACT:MpFRH1 lines and the gemma cups were generally empty (Figure 2N–P). Furthermore, like Mprsl1 loss-of-function mutants, MpFRH1GOF mutants and proACT:MpFRH1 lines lacked multicellular mucilage papillae (Figure 2Q–T).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic observations in Figure 2.

claim: MpFRH1 negatively regulates the development of the same structures (rhizoids, gemmae, and epidermal papillae) that are positively regulated by MpRSL1.
source: Together, these data suggest that MpFRH1 negatively regulates the development of the same structures – rhizoids, gemmae and epidermal papillae – that are positively regulated by MpRSL1.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of MpFRH1 gain-of-function and MpRSL1 loss-of-function phenotypes.

claim: There are no long open reading frames in the 1.2 kb MpFRH1 transcript sequence and the sequence is not similar to any Arabidopsis protein coding sequences.
source: There are no long open reading frames in the 1.2 kb MpFRH1 transcript sequence and the sequence is not similar to any Arabidopsis protein coding sequences.
evidence: Supported by bioinformatic sequence analysis.

claim: The 21 nt predicted miRNA mpo-MIR11861 (UGUGUGAGAAGAGGCCAAUGU) maps to the same genomic location as the MpFRH1 transcript.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the 21 nt predicted miRNA mpo-MIR11861 (UGUGUGAGAAGAGGCCAAUGU) maps to the same genomic location as the MpFRH1 transcript (Tsuzuki et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior miRNA prediction study.

claim: Over-expression of a 150 bp fragment of the MpFRH1 transcript containing the predicted miRNA hairpin structure in the wild type background was sufficient to reproduce the few rhizoids phenotype.
source: Over-expression of the 150 bp miRNA hairpin-containing fragment (MpFRH1miRNA) in the wild type background was sufficient to reproduce the few rhizoids phenotype (Figure 4C,I,O, Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by transformation experiments and phenotypic observations in Figure 4.

claim: The presence of the mature MpFRH1 miRNA was verified using stem-loop PCR.
source: The presence of the mature MpFRH1 miRNA was verified using stem-loop PCR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by stem-loop PCR experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elevated levels of the MpFRH1 pri-miRNA transcript in gain-of-function mutants give rise to elevated levels of mature MpFRH1 miRNA.
source: In the stem-loop PCR a 60 bp band corresponding to the MpFRH1 miRNA and a fused stem-loop sequence was stronger in the MpFRH1 gain-of-function mutant samples compared to wild type, suggesting that elevated levels of the MpFRH1 pri-miRNA transcript in these mutants give rise to elevated levels of mature MpFRH1 miRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from stem-loop PCR band intensity in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transformed plants over-expressing proACT:MpFRH1noATG (with mutated start codons) developed very few rhizoids similar to MpFRH1GOF lines and proACT:MpFRH1 lines.
source: Transformed plants over-expressing proACT:MpFRH1noATG developed very few rhizoids similar to the four MpFRH1GOF lines and proACT:MpFRH1 lines (Figure 4D,J,P, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by transformation experiments and phenotypic observations in Figure 4.

claim: Transformed plants overexpressing either MpFRH1PSORF1 or MpFRH1PSORF2 did not have defects in rhizoid development and were indistinguishable from wild type plants.
source: Transformed plants overexpressing either MpFRH1PSORF1 or MpFRH1PSORF2 did not have defects in rhizoid development and were undistinguishable from wild type plants (Figure 4E–F,K–L,Q–R, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by transformation experiments and phenotypic observations in Figure 4.

claim: MpFRH1 encodes a miRNA and not a peptide.
source: This is consistent with the hypothesis that the MpFRH1 transcript encodes a miRNA and not a peptide. Together, these findings indicate that MpFRH1 encodes a miRNA that represses rhizoid development.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing function with mutated start codons and lack of function of putative ORFs.

claim: Four putative MpFRH1 miRNA target mRNAs were identified using TargetFinder with default parameters.
source: We identified four putative MpFRH1 miRNA target mRNAs using TargetFinder with default parameters (Fahlgren and Carrington, 2010), TargetFinder. GitHub. https://github.com/carringtonlab/TargetFinder) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatic target prediction analysis.

claim: One of the predicted MpFRH1 miRNA targets was a 21 bp sequence on the MpRSL1 mRNA.
source: One of the predicted targets was a 21 bp sequence on the MpRSL1 mRNA.
evidence: Supported by bioinformatic target prediction analysis.

claim: The steady state levels of MpRSL1 mRNA were lower in all four MpFRH1GOF mutants and the four proACT1:MpFRH1 lines tested.
source: The steady state levels of MpRSL1 mRNA were lower in all four MpFRH1GOF mutants and the four proACT1:MpFRH1 lines tested (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3C.

claim: The amplified MpRSL1 mRNA fragment from 5'RLM-RACE PCR terminated within the predicted MpFRH1 target site, indicating MpFRH1 miRNA mediates cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA.
source: The amplified MpRSL1 mRNA fragment terminated within the predicted MpFRH1 target site (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 3), indicating MpFRH1 miRNA mediates cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA.
evidence: Supported by 5'RLM-RACE PCR experimental data in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The steady state levels of each of the three other predicted target mRNAs were similar in wild type and MpFRH1 gain of function mutants, suggesting they are not MpFRH1 miRNA targets.
source: The steady state levels of each of the three other predicted target mRNAs were similar in wild type and MpFRH1 gain of function mutants suggesting that they are not MpFRH1 miRNA targets (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The predicted MpFRH1 miRNA target site on the orthologs of the three other predicted targets is not conserved among liverworts.
source: Furthermore, the predicted MpFRH1 miRNA target site on the orthologs of each of these three mRNAs is not conserved among liverworts (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data in Supplementary file 4.

claim: MpFRH1 miRNA negatively regulates rhizoid development by mediating the cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA.
source: We conclude that MpFRH1 miRNA negatively regulates rhizoid development by mediating the cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA.
evidence: Inferred from 5'RLM-RACE PCR data showing cleavage and qRT-PCR data showing reduced MpRSL1 levels.

claim: Seven of ten transformed lines expressing MpFRH1 miRNA resistant version of MpRSL1 (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res) in the MpFRH1GOF2 background developed abundant rhizoids on the ventral thallus surface.
source: Seven of these transformed lines developed abundant rhizoids on the ventral thallus surface and two lines developed rhizoids on both ventral and dorsal surfaces of the thallus, while a single line was rhizoidless and was phenotypically identical to MpFRH1GOF2 plants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by transformation experiments and phenotypic observations in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: None (0%) of the gemmalings expressing the wild type MpRSL1 in the MpFRH1GOF2 background (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1wt MpFRH1GOF2) developed rhizoids.
source: None (0%) of the gemmalings expressing the wild type MpRSL1 in the MpFRH1GOF2 background (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1wt MpFRH1GOF2) developed rhizoids (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic scoring data in Figure 5.

claim: Most (88.9%) gemmalings transformed with the miRNA resistant form of MpRSL1 (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res MpFRH1GOF2) developed rhizoids.
source: In contrast, most (88.9%) gemmalings transformed with the miRNA resistant form of the MpRSL1 (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res MpFRH1GOF2) developed rhizoids (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic scoring data in Figure 5.

claim: Gemmae developed in the gemma cups of MpFRH1GOF2 plants transformed with proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res, while the gemma cups of proMpEF1α:MpRSL1wt MpFRH1GOF2 plants were mostly empty.
source: Gemmae developed in the gemma cups of MpFRH1GOF2 plants transformed with proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res, while similar to the MpFRH1GOF2 plants the gemma cups of proMpEF1α:MpRSL1wt MpFRH1GOF2 plants were mostly empty (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic observations in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The restoration of gemma development by the proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res construct in the MpFRH1GOF2 background demonstrates that MpRSL1 is a target of MpFRH1 regulation during gemma development.
source: The restoration of gemma development by the proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res construct in the MpFRH1GOF2 background demonstrates that MpRSL1 is a target of MpFRH1 regulation during gemma development.
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiments showing restoration of gemma development.

claim: MpFRH1 negatively regulates MpRSL1 by mediating the cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA during the development of structures derived from single epidermal cells in M. polymorpha.
source: Together these data are consistent with the hypothesis that MpFRH1 negatively regulates MpRSL1 by mediating the cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA during the development of structures derived from single epidermal cells in M. polymorpha.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence including cleavage assays and rescue experiments.

claim: Steady state MpFRH1 transcript levels were lower than wild type in the Mprsl1-1 and Mprsl1-2 loss-of-function mutant alleles.
source: Steady state MpFRH1 transcript levels were lower than wild type in the Mprsl1-1 and Mprsl1-2 loss-of-function mutant alleles, but higher than wild type in the MpRSL1 gain-of-function mutant alleles MpRSLGOF1-3 (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 6.

claim: MpRSL1 positively regulates steady state MpFRH1 transcript level.
source: These results indicate that MpRSL1 positively regulates steady state MpFRH1 transcript level.
evidence: Inferred from qRT-PCR data showing correlation between MpRSL1 and MpFRH1 levels.

claim: Functional MpRSL1 is not required for baseline MpFRH1 expression; a low level of MpFRH1 mRNA persists in the Mprsl1 complete loss-of-function mutant background.
source: However, functional MpRSL1 is not required for baseline MpFRH1 expression; a low level of MpFRH1 mRNA persists in the Mprsl1 complete loss-of-function mutant background (Figure 6)
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 6 showing residual MpFRH1 expression in Mprsl1 mutants.

claim: MpRSL1 and MpFRH1 miRNA form a regulatory loop with negative feedback.
source: The positive regulation of MpFRH1 expression by MpRSL1, which is in turn targeted by MpFRH1 miRNA, indicates that MpRSL1 and MpFRH1 miRNA form a regulatory loop with negative feedback.
evidence: Inferred from data showing MpRSL1 positively regulates MpFRH1 and MpFRH1 negatively regulates MpRSL1.

claim: YFP fluorescence, indicative of MpFRH1 promoter activity, was observed in rhizoid precursor cells.
source: We observed YFP fluorescence, indicative of MpFRH1 promoter activity, in the rhizoid precursor cells, which on young gemmae can be distinguished from non-rhizoid precursor cells based on their strongly reduced chlorophyll autofluorescence (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy observations in Figure 7.

claim: The YFP signal persisted in elongating rhizoids.
source: The YFP signal persisted in elongating rhizoids (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy observations in Figure 7.

claim: Strong MpFRH1 promoter activity was observed in mucilage papillae that form near the gemmae meristematic region of 1 day old gemmae.
source: In addition, we observed strong MpFRH1 promoter activity in mucilage papillae that form near the gemmae meristematic region of 1 day old gemmae (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy observations in Figure 7.

claim: Some mucilage papillae were observed without YFP signal, suggesting that MpFRH1 is transiently expressed during mucilage papilla development.
source: We also observed some mucilage papillae without YFP signal, suggesting that MpFRH1 is transiently expressed during mucilage papilla development.
evidence: Inferred from observation of variable YFP signal in mucilage papillae.

claim: MpFRH1 is expressed in epidermal cells that develop rhizoids and papillae.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that MpFRH1 is expressed in epidermal cells that develop rhizoids and papillae.
evidence: Inferred from promoter-reporter expression patterns.

claim: The FRH1 miRNA binding site is 100% conserved in all twelve liverwort species for which RSL class I transcript sequence data was available through the 1000 plants project.
source: The FRH1 miRNA binding site is 100% conserved in all twelve liverwort species for which RSL class I transcript sequence data was available through the 1000 plants project (https://db.cngb.org/onekp/, Figure 8, a longer region of the alignment is provided in Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The twelve liverwort species with conserved FRH1 miRNA binding sites belong to Marchantiopsida and Jugermanniopsida; two of the three major liverwort lineages.
source: These twelve liverwort species belong to Marchantiopsida and Jugermanniopsida; two of the three major liverwort lineages (sequence data for RSL class I transcripts in the third major liverwort lineage Haplomitriopsida was not available) (Forrest et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by taxonomic classification and citation to phylogenetic study.

claim: There is no MpFRH1 binding site sequence in the class I RSL transcripts of the moss P. patens, the lycophyte S. kraussiana, or the angiosperm A. thaliana.
source: There is no MpFRH1 binding site sequence in the class I RSL transcripts of the moss P. patens, the lycophyte S. Kraussiana or the angiosperm A. thaliana.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis of RSL class I transcripts from these species.

claim: While the regulation of RSL class I genes by FRH1-like miRNAs became established early in the liverwort lineage, different negative regulation evolved in other lineages.
source: Together, these data suggest that while the regulation of RSL class I genes by FRH1-like miRNAs became established early in the liverwort lineage, different negative regulation evolved in other lineages.
evidence: Inferred from conservation pattern showing FRH1 target site only in liverworts.

claim: The genomic sequence 3.5 kb upstream of MpRSL1 does not contain any L1-box sequences.
source: The genomic sequence 3.5 kb upstream of MpRSL1 does not contain any L1-box sequences.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis of MpRSL1 promoter region.

claim: The MpFRH1 miRNA negatively regulates MpRSL1 in M. polymorpha and there is no evidence for a role of class IV homeodomain protein in the negative regulation of MpRSL1 expression.
source: Therefore, the MpFRH1 miRNA negatively regulates MpRSL1 in M. polymorpha and we find no evidence for a role of class IV homeodomain protein in the negative regulation of MpRSL1 expression.
evidence: Inferred from absence of L1-box sequences and experimental evidence for miRNA regulation.

claim: Different mechanisms of negative regulation of RSL class I transcription factors evolved in liverworts and angiosperms.
source: The discovery that a miRNA represses RSL class I function in liverworts demonstrates that different mechanisms of negative regulation of these conserved transcription factors evolved in the liverworts and angiosperms.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of miRNA-based regulation in liverworts versus GL2-based regulation in Arabidopsis.

claim: AtGL2 is the only repressor of AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 to have been identified to date.
source: To date, AtGL2 is the only repressor of AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 to have been identified.
evidence: Statement about current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: There are no FRH1 miRNA target sequences in either AtRHD6 or AtRSL1 mRNA and the FRH1 miRNA has not been identified in A. thaliana or any other angiosperm.
source: There are no FRH1 miRNA target sequences in either AtRHD6 or AtRSL1 mRNA and the FRH1 miRNA has not been identified in A. thaliana or any other angiosperm.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and literature review.

claim: At least two independent mechanisms that negatively regulate the ancient RSL class I gene mediated differentiation module have evolved among land plants.
source: The observation that RSL class I genes are repressed by a miRNA and a homeodomain-leucine-zipper transcription factor in M. polymorpha and A. thaliana respectively demonstrates that at least two independent mechanisms that negatively regulate the ancient RSL class I gene mediated differentiation module have evolved among land plants.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of regulatory mechanisms in liverworts and Arabidopsis.

claim: Different modes of negative regulation for RSL class I genes have likely evolved more than twice during the course of land plant evolution.
source: It is likely that different modes of negative regulation for RSL class I genes have evolved more than twice during the course of land plant evolution.
evidence: Speculative inference based on absence of known regulatory mechanisms in other lineages.

claim: The FRH1 miRNA target sites are not conserved in RSL class I mRNAs of P. patens, O. sativa, or B. distachyon, and FRH1 miRNA has not been identified in either mosses or grasses.
source: The FRH1 miRNA target sites are not conserved in these RSL class I mRNAs and FRH1 miRNA has not been identified in either mosses or grasses.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and literature review.

claim: The FRH1 miRNA is unlikely to act as negative regulator outside the liverworts.
source: Therefore, the FRH1 miRNA is unlikely to act as negative regulator outside the liverworts.
evidence: Inferred from lack of conservation of target sites and absence of miRNA in other lineages.

claim: MpFRH1 miRNA is only found in one monophyletic lineage of land plants, the liverworts.
source: MpFRH1 miRNA is only found in one monophyletic lineage of land plants, the liverworts.
evidence: Supported by sequence conservation analysis across land plant lineages.

claim: The FRH1 miRNA has been conserved since the divergence of the two major clades of liverworts (Marchantiopsida and Jungermanniopsida), estimated to have occurred more than 405 million years ago.
source: It has been conserved since the divergence of the two major clades of liverworts – Marchantiopsida and Jungermanniopsida – estimated to have occurred more than 405 million years ago (Morris et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by sequence conservation data and citation to phylogenetic dating study.

claim: The FRH1 miRNA may have existed since soon after the divergence of liverworts from other land plant lineages approximately 440 million years ago.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the FRH1 miRNA may have existed since soon after the divergence of liverworts from other land plant lineages approximately 440 million years ago (Morris et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculative inference based on conservation pattern and phylogenetic dating.

claim: The appearance of the FRH1 miRNA may have been associated with gene regulatory network rewiring that occurred during the morphological diversification early in the liverwort lineage or during the evolution of liverworts from a common, non-liverwort ancestor.
source: The appearance of the FRH1 miRNA may have been associated with gene regulatory network rewiring that occurred during the morphological diversification early in the liverwort lineage or during the evolution of liverworts from a common, non-liverwort ancestor.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis about evolutionary significance.

claim: Many transcription factor families previously thought to have evolved within land plants were already established in streptophyte algae.
source: However, recent studies demonstrate that many transcription factor families previously thought to have evolved within land plants were already established in streptophyte algae (Wilhelmsson et al., 2017; Hori et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on transcription factor evolution.

claim: The evolution of morphologically complex land plants from algal ancestors is likely to have involved the emergence of novel negative regulatory mechanisms around a core set of ancient transcription factors resulting in the evolution of novel gene regulatory networks that programmed novel morphologies.
source: The evolution of morphologically complex land plants from these algal ancestors is likely to have involved the emergence of novel negative regulatory mechanisms – such as miRNAs and transcriptional repressor proteins – around this core set of ancient transcription factors resulting in the evolution of novel gene regulatory networks that programmed novel morphologies.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: The evolution of new and distinct negative regulatory mechanisms in different lineages may have underpinned the radiation of morphological diversity in the stem groups of the major lineages of land plants.
source: Furthermore, the evolution of new and distinct negative regulatory mechanisms in the different lineages may have underpinned the radiation of morphological diversity in the stem groups of the major lineages of land plants.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: The radiation in morphological diversity between the Ordovician and Late Devonian may have resulted, at least in part, from the evolution of novel negative regulatory activities that modulated more ancient and conserved gene regulatory networks.
source: If correct, it suggests that the radiation in morphological diversity between the Ordovician and Late Devonian resulted, at least in part, from the evolution of novel negative regulatory activities that modulated more ancient and conserved gene regulatory networks that are conserved in many extant land plant lineages.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis about evolutionary mechanisms.
